entries.topic: The Arab Revolt, 1936–1939: phases, British counterinsurgency, Palestinian divisions, and the death toll

claims.text: Izz al-Din al-Qassam was killed by British forces in November 1935; the killing preceded the revolt and is named by historians as part of its background.

On 15 April 1936 Palestinian Arabs killed two Jews near Tulkarm; Jewish retaliation followed and riots broke out in Jaffa and Tel Aviv. The Jewish Virtual Library describes the attack as one on a Jewish bus and gives three Jewish dead.

The strike began with a call on 19 April 1936 from a newly formed Arab National Committee in Nablus for a general strike, the withholding of taxes and a boycott of Jewish products; local national committees then united on 25 April as the Arab Higher Committee.

The Arab Higher Committee was formed on 25 April 1936 under Hajj Amin al-Husseini, Mufti of Jerusalem, and declared a general strike with three demands: an end to Jewish immigration, an end to land sales to Jews, and an independent national government.

The Arab Higher Committee's founding members, as listed from the Peel report, joined the leaders of the rival clans and parties: Amin al-Husseini (president), Raghib al-Nashashibi (National Defence Party), Jamal al-Husseini (Palestine Arab Party), Yaqub al-Ghusayn (Youth Congress), Abd al-Latif Salah (National Bloc), Husayn al-Khalidi (Reform Party), Awni Abd al-Hadi (Istiqlal, general secretary) and Ahmed Hilmi Pasha (treasurer). Raghib al-Nashashibi left soon after.

The general strike lasted about six months. On 12 October 1936 the British General Officer Commanding issued a Special Order stating that the strike and armed rebellion had been 'called off unconditionally by the Higher Arab Committee'; the rulers of neighbouring Arab states (named in different sources as Transjordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Yemen) had mediated its end.

The same British Special Order of October 1936 counted, for the strike period, 25 British soldiers killed and 120 wounded, 7 British police killed and 40 wounded, 9 Palestine police killed and 64 wounded, and a total cost of the rebellion of at least 300 dead and 1,300 wounded.

The second phase began in autumn 1937 after District Commissioner Lewis Andrews was killed in Nazareth in September 1937; the revolt moved into the countryside, where rebel bands set up their own administration and taxed peasants, and it peaked in autumn 1938, when rebels held large parts of the country, before being suppressed by summer 1939.

On 26 September 1937 four gunmen described as followers of Izz al-Din al-Qassam killed Lewis Andrews, District Commissioner for Galilee, as he left a service at Christ Church, Nazareth; his police bodyguard died of wounds. Within 24 hours police had detained about 100 Palestinian Arabs.

After the killing Britain outlawed the Arab Higher Committee (about 30 September 1937), stripped al-Husseini of his offices, arrested committee members and deported several to the Seychelles. Al-Husseini took refuge in the Haram al-Sharif and escaped in the autumn of 1937 (to Lebanon, according to Unpacked; to Syria, according to the Jewish Virtual Library), from where, by Unpacked's account, he authorized attacks on Britons, Jews and Palestinians considered collaborators.

Britain sent about 20,000 troops. Its measures included house demolitions, executions, outlawing the Arab Higher Committee, arrests and expulsions of activists, indefinite detention, collective fines on neighbourhoods and the disarming of Palestinians; Matthew Hughes's 2019 study groups the methods into eight categories.
Between 108 and 122 Palestinian Arabs were hanged in the 1930s, against 1,090 Kenyans hanged during the Mau Mau emergency of the 1950s, the comparison Hughes's reviewer draws; two Jews were hanged.

Jewish attacks on Arab civilians are part of the record: in November 1937 the Irgun abandoned the policy of restraint and killed ten Arab civilians on what was later called 'Black Sunday'; after an attack on an Arab bus in April 1938, Shlomo Ben-Yosef was hanged by the British in June 1938, one of two Jews hanged; by Unpacked's count at least 250 Palestinian Arabs had died at Irgun hands by summer 1939.

Raghib al-Nashashibi, former mayor of Jerusalem, favoured compromise with the British while the Mufti opposed it; the rivalry produced hundreds of killings of Palestinians by Palestinians, and the Nashashibi-aligned 'peace bands' were raised with British and Jewish military and financial help to fight the rebels.

Peace bands in detail (Hughes 2016): Fakhri Nashashibi was organizing them from Lebanon by March 1938; Fakhri 'Abd al-Hadi, a former rebel commander, returned to Palestine on 21 September 1938 with British consular backing from Damascus (Gilbert MacKereth); Britain paid band members £P6 a month, against 30 shillings to £P4 for insurgents. Husseini-backed gunmen killed Fakhri Nashashibi in Iraq in 1941; 'Abd al-Hadi was murdered in 1943.

Hughes concludes that the peace bands 'never won the war for the British', that collaboration was driven more by survival, personal gain and feuds than by political conviction, and that 'Palestinian collaboration in the 1930s was too partial to damn the Arab revolt.'

Arab deaths: Walid Khalidi's analysis of British statistics gives 3,832 Palestinian Arabs killed by the British and 1,200 killed in internal strife (5,032 in all), with 14,760 wounded; official British figures give over 2,000 Arabs killed in combat, 108 hanged and 961 killed by 'gang and terrorist activities'. Reference works round the total to about 5,000.

Jewish and British deaths are given differently: about 415 Jews and 100 British (Yehudai, Origins); 415 Jewish deaths for 1936–39 (Jewish Virtual Library); nearly 400 Jews and 200 Britons (Strickert, EBSCO); 'hundreds' of Jews (Hughes's reviewer). None of the sources fetched gives the figures of 2,652 Jews and 618 British used elsewhere in the library.

Middle East Eye gives the revolt's Palestinian toll as about 5,000 killed, 15,000–20,000 wounded and 5,600 imprisoned, and describes the revolt as 'the most sustained armed resistance' against the Mandate; Unpacked (Noam Weissman, 2024), drawing on Oren Kessler, gives 5,000–8,000 Palestinian Arab dead and says about 20 percent of Palestinian Arab men were jailed at some point.

The Jewish Virtual Library estimates Arab losses at roughly 5,000 dead, 15,000 wounded and 5,600 imprisoned; the Palestinian church committee's summary states that over 10 percent of Palestinian Arab men aged 20 to 60 were killed, wounded, imprisoned or exiled.
About 40,000 Christian Arabs and others moved to Syria and Lebanon during the revolt, according to the review of Hughes's study.

Historians agree on the outcome: the revolt failed militarily, the Palestinian leadership was left weak, divided and in exile, British–Zionist military cooperation deepened, and the general strike pushed the Yishuv toward a more self-reliant economy.

disputes.question: How many people died in the revolt?

positions.view: Khalidi, from British statistics: 5,032 Arab dead (3,832 by the British, 1,200 in internal strife) and 14,760 wounded.
Official British figures: over 2,000 Arabs killed in combat, 108 hanged, 961 killed by 'gang and terrorist activities'.
Reference-work rounding: about 5,000 Arabs, 400–415 Jews and 100–200 British.
Higher ranges in popular and press accounts: 5,000–8,000 Palestinian Arab dead (Unpacked, after Kessler); 5,000 killed and 15,000–20,000 wounded (Middle East Eye).
The appeal of the Arab rulers, with British concessions and the threat of martial law.
Economic pressure, especially the approaching citrus harvest, is also cited by historians alongside the rulers' appeal.

disputes.question: How to characterize the revolt and its internal violence

positions.view: A national uprising and 'the most sustained armed resistance' against the Mandate, crushed by brutal British repression (Middle East Eye).
An uprising whose rebels also turned on Palestinians, extorting and killing those deemed disloyal, with leaders encouraging it (Unpacked).
Scholarly synthesis: collaboration and internal killing were real but 'too partial to damn the Arab revolt' (Hughes).

entries.topic: From Peel to St James's Palace: partition proposed, tested and dropped, 1936–1939

claims.text: The Palestine Royal Commission (the Peel Commission) had six members and was appointed in August 1936, during the general strike.

Its July 1937 report proposed ending the Mandate and creating an independent Arab state of Transjordan joined to part of Palestine, and an independent Jewish state in another part, with Jerusalem and some other places kept under British mandate.
The size of the proposed Jewish state is given as 17 percent of the country (Yehudai, Origins) or about 20 percent (Strickert, EBSCO).
The transfer figures are rounded differently: about 200,000 Arabs and about 1,000 Jews (Yehudai) or about 225,000 Palestinians against 1,250 Jews (Middle East Eye).

The Twentieth Zionist Congress (1937) rejected the proposed boundaries but accepted partition in principle; the Arab side rejected the plan. A United Nations working paper of 1949 summarizes the result as rejection by both Jews and Arabs.
Peel's partition proposal prompted rebel groups to restart the revolt in the autumn of 1937.

Britain then sent a four-member technical commission under Sir John Woodhead to test whether partition could be carried out; its members were Woodhead, Sir Alison Russell, Percival Waterfield and Thomas Reid, and it investigated in Palestine from April to early August 1938.

The Woodhead (Palestine Partition) Commission reported on 9 November 1938 with three boundary plans, A, B and C; it preferred Plan C, proposed that the two states stay in a customs union with the Mandatory government, and questioned the economic and political viability of partition.

The commission concluded that no practical partition plan could be devised because both Jews and Arabs refused it, and the British government accepted its conclusion that partition was politically, administratively and financially impossible.

Britain invited the Palestinian Arabs, neighbouring Arab states and the Jewish Agency to a conference in London in early 1939 (the St James's Palace conference). The Arab Higher Committee delegation refused to sit with the Zionist delegation, so the British held separate meetings with each side.

The Palestinian delegation was led by Jamal al-Husseini and included Awni Abd al-Hadi, Musa al-Alami and others, with George Antonius as a secretary; Raghib al-Nashashibi joined two days after the opening. Egypt, Iraq (Prime Minister Nuri al-Said) and Saudi Arabia (Prince Faisal) also sent delegations. The Jewish Agency delegation was led by Chaim Weizmann, with Ben-Gurion dominant in its decisions, and included non-Zionists and Rabbi Stephen Wise.

An Anglo-Arab committee under the Lord Chancellor, Lord Maugham, examined the Hussein–McMahon correspondence during the conference; it found the Arab case had been given too little weight but the two sides could not agree whether Palestine had been included in the pledge.

The White Paper itself records the result: after talks lasting several weeks, 'Neither the Arab nor the Jewish delegation felt able to accept these proposals, and the conferences failed to reach an agreement.'

disputes.question: Did the Zionist movement accept Peel?

positions.view: It accepted partition in principle while rejecting the boundaries (Jewish Virtual Library).
Both sides rejected the plan (UN Conciliation Commission working paper, 1949).

entries.topic: The White Paper of May 1939: text, reception and legality

claims.text: The White Paper (Palestine: Statement of Policy, Cmd 6019) is dated 17 May 1939; Parliament approved the policy on 23 May.

It declared that 'it is not part of their policy that Palestine should become a Jewish State' and stated as its objective 'the establishment within ten years of an independent Palestine State' in treaty relations with the United Kingdom, after a transitional period, with a review body to be set up five years after the restoration of peace and order.

Immigration: 'some 75,000 immigrants over the next five years' — a quota of 10,000 Jewish immigrants a year for five years plus 25,000 refugees to be admitted when the High Commissioner was satisfied provision could be made for them; illegal immigrants were to be deducted from the yearly quotas.

After five years, 'no further Jewish immigration will be permitted unless the Arabs of Palestine are prepared to acquiesce in it'; the effect, as Churchill quoted the paper in the Commons, was to bring the Jewish population to approximately one-third of the total.
Land: 'the High Commissioner will be given general powers to prohibit and regulate transfers of land.'

In the Commons debate of 22–23 May 1939, Leo Amery called the policy a repudiation of Britain's pledges; Churchill called it 'an act of repudiation' and said he would vote against; Labour's Herbert Morrison called it 'a cynical breach of pledges given to the Jews and the world, including America' and urged referral to the Permanent Mandates Commission.

On 31 May 1939 Weizmann wrote to the High Commissioner that the White Paper meant 'denying to the Jewish people the right to reconstitute their National Home in Palestine'; the Jewish Agency's legal memorandum to the Permanent Mandates Commission argued that it breached Articles 2, 6 and 15 of the Mandate and that an Arab veto on immigration could not be squared with the duty to 'facilitate Jewish immigration'.

The US consul general in Jerusalem, George Wadsworth, reported in early June 1939 that the ten-year state was broadly acceptable to Arabs and strongly opposed by Zionists; Jews responded with bitterness and 'a sullen determination to continue' building the national home, while Arabs showed 'very obvious relief' but distrusted British intentions and resented the indefinite ban on the Mufti's return.

The Arab Higher Committee nevertheless rejected the White Paper, demanding a complete prohibition of Jewish immigration; Benny Morris attributes al-Husseini's rejection in part to the plan not placing him at the head of the future state. (Reported via a secondary summary; Morris's text not read directly.)

The Permanent Mandates Commission considered the White Paper at its 36th session, 8–29 June 1939. It held unanimously that the policy was not in accordance with the interpretation it had always placed on the Mandate; by a majority of one (four members to three) it found it could not say the policy conformed to the Mandate, the minority holding that circumstances could justify it if the League Council did not object.
War broke out before the League Council could act, so the White Paper never came before it.

In July 1939, citing illegal immigration, Britain suspended the next six-month quota of controlled Jewish immigration; in the Commons debate of 20 July Malcolm MacDonald said it 'would have been a breach of that policy' not to suspend it.

After the war began, Ben-Gurion set the Yishuv's line: help the British army 'as if there were no White Paper' and fight the White Paper 'as if there were no war'. (Wording as given in a secondary summary; the original source has not been read.)

disputes.question: Was the White Paper consistent with the Mandate?

positions.view: No: the Jewish Agency, Labour's Morrison, Churchill and the majority of the Permanent Mandates Commission (four of seven).
Yes, or justifiable in the circumstances: the British government, which carried the Commons, and the Commission's minority of three.

disputes.question: How did Palestinian Arabs receive it?

positions.view: With evident relief at its provisions, according to the US consul general's contemporary report.
The Arab Higher Committee formally rejected it as offering only illusory independence.

entries.topic: Labour and Palestine, 1939–1945: the party that came to power in July 1945

claims.text: A State Department Near Eastern Affairs memorandum signed by William Yale, dated 30 July 1945, assessed the new Labour government's likely Palestine policy for the Potsdam conference.

It recorded that Labour leaders, Labour MPs and the major unions 'have consistently given their support to the Balfour Declaration', and that in 1939 Labour members had argued that the White Paper's limits on immigration and land transfers were 'contrary to the terms of the Mandate'.

Clement Attlee, who became Prime Minister in July 1945, had voted against the 1939 White Paper; so had Hugh Dalton. Herbert Morrison had said the government should not adopt a policy 'as to which grave doubt exists as to its consistency with the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate'.

The Labour Party conference of December 1944 adopted a resolution saying there was no case for a Jewish national home 'unless we are prepared to let Jews, if they wish, enter this tiny land in such numbers as to become a majority', and adding: 'Let the Arabs be encouraged to move out, as the Jews move in'; it also proposed re-examining 'the possibility of extending the present Palestinian boundaries'.

Yale expected the Labour government not to try to implement that resolution, but to 'modify or repeal the White Paper policy of 1939', especially on immigration, because the remaining quota would soon be exhausted, and to consult the Soviet and American governments before deciding Palestine's future status.

entries.topic: The Holocaust in primary documents: perpetrator records, trial evidence and the liberation record

claims.text: The Wannsee Protocol records a conference held on 20 January 1942; the minutes were compiled and heavily edited by Adolf Eichmann from notes taken at the meeting and are not a word-for-word transcript.
The minutes were made in 30 copies; the stamp on the surviving copy reads '30 copies' and '16th copy', and copy no. 16 belonged to Undersecretary Martin Luther of the German Foreign Office.

The House of the Wannsee Conference states there were 30 copies of the protocol, only one has been found, and it was discovered by American soldiers in a file together with 300 other pieces of evidence among Foreign Office files seized from external storage (photo: Schloss Meisdorf, 19 April 1945).

According to USHMM, the copy came to light among the Foreign Office files in late 1946, when American microfilming staff member Kenneth Duke found it and alerted Dr. Robert Kempner in March 1947; it was first submitted as evidence in 1947 in the Ministries Trial (NMT Case 11).

The protocol's country table totals 'over 11,000,000' Jews, listing among others the General Government at 2,284,000, Bialystok at 400,000, the USSR at 5,000,000, England at 330,000, and Estonia as 'free of Jews'.
The surviving protocol (item R 100857) is reproduced courtesy of the Politisches Archiv des Auswärtigen Amts (Political Archive of the German Foreign Office).

The Höfle telegram, intercepted on 11 January 1943, was sent by SS-Sturmbannführer Höfle, SS and police leader staff in Lublin (Globocnik's adjutant), and reported, as of 31 December 1942, arrivals of L (Majdanek) 24,733, B (Belzec) 434,508, S (Sobibor) 101,370 and T (Treblinka) 713,555, a total of 1,274,166.
The decrypt text as held by The National Archives (UK) shows Treblinka as 71,355, a figure the archive notes is missing a digit; with 713,555 the four camp figures sum to the stated 1,274,166.
The telegram's fortnightly figures (last two weeks of 1942) were L 12,761, B 0, S 515 and T 10,335, totalling 23,611.
The decrypt was one of many German police messages decoded at Bletchley Park and is held at The National Archives, Kew, in GC&CS records under catalogue reference HW 16/23 (January 1943).

The National Archives and Holocaust Denial on Trial state the decrypt was discovered in 2000 among newly declassified records; Sobibor.org dates the discovery to 2001 and cites its publication by historians P. Witte and S. Tyas in Holocaust and Genocide Studies, vol. 14-3 (2001), pp. 468-486.

Heinrich Himmler commissioned SS statistician Richard Korherr to write 'The Final Solution of the European Jewish Question'; USHMM states Korherr finished it in January 1943 and gave it to Dr. Rudolf Brandt in March, with a summary later passed to Hitler.
USHMM acquired Korherr's personal papers (Accession 2021.201.1, 6,142 digital images), which contain two copies of the Korherr report.
The Korherr report (Yad Vashem translation dated 23 March 1943) gives total evacuations 'including Theresienstadt and Special Treatment' of 1,873,549, or 1,786,356 without Theresienstadt.

Himmler ordered that the term 'Sonderbehandlung' (special treatment) of the Jews not be used; Korherr was told to substitute wording meaning 'processed through the camps in the Government-General' ('durchgeschleust'), though one 'Special Treatment' instance remained in the final version.

Holocaust Denial on Trial reports that the Korherr report repeats Höfle's exact figure of 1,274,166 for the four Reinhard camps and that its figures for French (41,911) and Belgian (16,886) Jews closely match transport lists (41,941 and 16,861).

A set of 195 Operational Situation Reports USSR (Ereignismeldungen), covering June 1941 to 1 May 1942 and circulated across German government branches including the Wehrmacht, was found on 3 September 1945 on the fourth floor of Gestapo headquarters in Berlin by the 6889th Berlin Document Group.

At the Einsatzgruppen trial the prosecution cited Operational Situation Report No. 128 stating 'approximately 80,000 persons were liquidated until now by the Kommandos' and Report No. 106 stating approximately 35,000 Jews of Kiev were killed on 29-30 September 1941, while another report gave Sonderkommando 4a's Kiev figure as 33,771.

The Jäger Report, signed by SS-Standartenführer Karl Jäger, commander of Einsatzkommando 3, at Kovno on 1 December 1941, states that there are no more Jews in Lithuania apart from working Jews and their families; Yad Vashem holds it as YVA O-18/245.
The Jäger Report's running tally ends 'Total 137,346', covering 21 June to 1 December 1941 across 113 operations in 71 locations; the original is held in the Central Lithuanian Archives in Vilnius.

NMT Case 9 (Einsatzgruppen Case) indicted 24 defendants led by Otto Ohlendorf; 22 were tried, the trial ran from 29 September 1947 to 12 February 1948, and prosecutor Benjamin Ferencz relied on wartime SS reports rather than witnesses.
On 10 April 1948 the tribunal sentenced 14 defendants to death, 2 to life and 5 to 10-20 years; only four death sentences (Ohlendorf, Naumann, Blobel, Braune) were carried out, on 7 June 1951.

The Stroop Report is an album prepared by SS Major General Jürgen Stroop documenting the suppression of the Warsaw Ghetto uprising (19 April-16 May 1943); three albums were made (for Himmler, Krüger and Stroop) and copies are held at the US National Archives, the Bundesarchiv and Poland's Institute of National Remembrance.
Stroop's teletype of 16 May 1943 reports 'Total number of Jews dealt with 56,065, including both Jews caught and Jews whose extermination can be proved.'

The Bundesarchiv states its copy of the Stroop Report was held shortly after the war by SHAEF and was received by the Bundesarchiv in 2005 from the British Foreign Office Research Department's 'German Collection'; the copy used at Nuremberg is in the US National Archives.

The US National Archives holds Himmler's handwritten notes for his 4 October 1943 speech to SS generals, which use the euphemism 'Judenevakuierung', and states that in sound recordings of the speech Himmler defined 'evacuation' as 'extermination'.

In the 4 October 1943 Posen speech (Nuremberg document 1919-PS), Himmler spoke of 'the extermination (Ausrottung) of the Jewish people' as a never-to-be-written page of glory; a transcript runs to 116 pages.

In affidavit 3868-PS, signed at Nuremberg on 5 April 1946, Rudolf Höss estimated 'at least 2,500,000 victims were executed and exterminated' at Auschwitz by gassing and burning and 'at least another half million succumbed to starvation and disease making a total dead of about 3,000,000'.

Testifying before the IMT on 15 April 1946, Höss confirmed the affidavit's contents as true and agreed that Eichmann had told him more than 2 million Jews had been destroyed at Auschwitz; he stated he was commander at Auschwitz from May 1940 until December 1943.

The Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum states that Höss's figures were 'highly overinflated' (as Höss himself later said in Polish custody), that Franciszek Piper's 1990 research gave 1.1 million as the most probable number of victims, and that about 1.3 million people were deported to Auschwitz, about 1.1 million of whom were murdered.

Eichmann's trial (Jerusalem District Court criminal case 40/61) opened on 11 April 1961; 1,600 documents were selected as evidence, most bearing Eichmann's signature, and a list of 108 survivor witnesses was prepared.
Eichmann was sentenced to death on 15 December 1961 and hanged on 1 June 1962 at Ramla prison.

At the IMT on 22 November 1945, Col. Robert Storey testified that 'literally hundreds of tons of enemy documents and records were screened and examined' and that more than 2,500 documents were selected and filed at the Nuremberg courthouse, with originals kept in safes in the Document Room.

US documents were given trial identification numbers in one of five letter series indicating the means of acquisition (including L, R, C and EC; documents such as 2903-PS carry the PS suffix), and Maj. Coogan's affidavit of 19 November 1945 (001-A-PS, Exhibit USA-1) certified photostats as true copies of the originals.

USHMM states that the Allies presented roughly 3,000 tons of documents and records at Nuremberg, collected from millions of Nazi documents seized in 1945, and that a 1958 National Archives catalog of captured records ran to 62 volumes.

Nuremberg records are in US National Archives Record Group 238; captured-document series were microfilmed, including NG (T1139, 70 rolls), NI (T301, 164 rolls) and NOKW (T1119, 47 rolls), and the IMT proceedings were published in 42 volumes.

Captured records were microfilmed in the early 1950s by the Department of the Army with the American Historical Association before originals were returned; by March 1968 the Army had returned 35 shipments to Germany.

On 29 November 1945 the IMT prosecution, introduced by US prosecutor Thomas Dodd, showed an hour-long film, 'The Nazi Concentration Camps', compiled from footage shot as Allied troops liberated the camps, with clips credited to George Stevens.

Eisenhower visited Ohrdruf on 12 April 1945 with Patton and Bradley; that day he cabled Gen. George C. Marshall that 'The things I saw beggar description', and on 19 April asked Marshall to bring members of Congress and editors to the camps so the evidence could not be dismissed as propaganda.
The Arolsen Archives were founded by the Allies as the International Tracing Service in 1948, hold information on about 17.5 million people, and are part of UNESCO's Memory of the World.
In May 2006 the 11-nation International Commission agreed to amend the 1955 Bonn Accords, and the ITS archives, then described as some 50 million documents, opened to the public on 28 November 2007.

USHMM states the European rail network played a crucial role in the Final Solution, with the Transport Ministry organizing train schedules and millions transported by rail to killing centers between autumn 1941 and autumn 1944.

disputes.question: How many people died at Auschwitz?

positions.view: Höss affidavit 3868-PS (5 April 1946), confirmed in IMT testimony: at least 2,500,000 gassed and burned plus at least 500,000 from starvation and disease, about 3,000,000 total.
Höss affidavit of 14 May 1946: 2 million Jews gassed and 500,000 killed by other means.
Auschwitz Museum (Piper 1990, current consensus): about 1.3 million deported, about 1.1 million murdered; Soviet 4 million figure and Höss's figures overinflated.

disputes.question: Who found the Wannsee Protocol and when?

positions.view: Found by American soldiers among seized Foreign Office files (seizure April 1945).
Found in late 1946 by microfilming staffer Kenneth Duke, who alerted Kempner in March 1947.
Found by prosecutor Robert Kempner in 1947.

disputes.question: When was the Höfle decrypt discovered, and to whom was the telegram addressed?

positions.view: Discovered 2000; the Kew decrypt is addressed to SS-Obersturmbannführer Heim, Commander of Security Police, Cracow.
Discovered 2001 (publication year); HDOT says it was sent to Eichmann in Berlin (implying a parallel message).

disputes.question: Warsaw Ghetto total in the Stroop Report

positions.view: 56,065 'dealt with' (teletype 16 May 1943).
USHMM summaries: 'some 56,000' killed or captured; 'more than 55,000' captured of whom at least 7,000 killed.

disputes.question: Victim count attributed to the Case 9 defendants

positions.view: Indictment: between 723,661 and one million.
Prosecution estimate: more than one million.
Found guilty 11-12 December 1961, sentenced 15 December.
Yad Vashem: trial ended 15 December 1961 with reading of the verdict; elsewhere gives 13 December for the guilty finding.
